items.question: How did you think about establishing whether AlphaGo was truly as strong as you believed?
items.object: Assessing AlphaGo’s strength and blind spots
items.answer: Go is a complex game, and there was always a bit of worry about whether AlphaGo was truly as good as we believed. We had the conviction that deep reinforcement learning is the answer, based on everything we could measure and see. But these systems aren't like classic computers where you know they always produce the same answer. They're stochastic, they're creative, and they have some blind spots. They hallucinate similarly to how language models hallucinate, so you need to really push them and see exactly where they break. The only way you could do that is by having the best humans playing against them.

items.question: Why do you see video games as a useful testing ground for artificial general intelligence?
items.object: Video games as a testing ground for artificial general intelligence
items.answer: I think DeepMind was the first company to truly embrace the concept of artificial general intelligence, or AGI, from the outset. They had grand ambitions, aiming to build systems that would match or exceed human intelligence. The big question was, and still is, how do you build AGI? More importantly, how do you measure intelligence in a way that allows for meaningful research and performance improvements? The idea of using video games as a testing ground came naturally to DeepMind's founders. Demis had a background in the gaming industry, and Shane's PhD thesis defined AGI as a system that could learn to complete any task. Video games provided a controlled yet complex environment where these ideas could be explored and tested.

items.question: How do you assess the value and limitations of games as a testbed for developing AI for the real world?
items.object: Games as a testbed for developing AI
items.answer: Games have indeed been valuable for developing AI, and you have a few examples of that. PPO, for example, which is currently being used in RLHF, was developed using OpenAI Gym and MuJoCo. Similarly, MCTS, which stands for Monte Carlo Tree Search, was developed through board games like Go. But at the same time, games have a number of limitations. The real world is messy and unbounded. It's a much tougher nut to crack than even the most complex games. Even though games give you an interesting testbed to develop new ideas, I think it is limiting and doesn't really capture all the complexity of the real world.

items.question: Why do you see solving Go as such an important challenge for AI research?
items.object: Go as a challenge for AI research
items.answer: The way I see it, Go is a much harder problem than chess. It's almost completely impossible to define an evaluation method, a heuristic. In chess, you can look at the board, count the number of pawns each side has, see what the ranks of these pawns are, and draw conclusions about who is winning and why. In Go, there's nothing like that. It's mostly human intuition. If you ask a professional Go player how they know whether a position is good or bad, they'll say that after having played the game for so long, they can see in their gut that this is a better position than the other one. So now it's a question of how do you encode that feeling in your gut into an AI system? This is exactly why solving Go was considered the Holy Grail of AI research for a long time. It was a challenge that seemed almost impossible, but at the same time within reach. People felt they could get it cracked, and this is exactly what AlphaGo did back in 2016. It showcased two new methods: deep learning and reinforcement learning. Back in 2015 and 2016, these were taking their first steps, the new kid on the block. Most people were skeptical about them. Everyone thought deep learning was another AI fad that wouldn't last the test of time.

items.question: How do you think about the way AlphaGo uses its neural networks to imagine possible futures and choose a move?
items.object: AlphaGo's neural networks and planning
items.answer:
AlphaGo has two deep neural networks. A neural network is a function that takes something as an input and produces something as an output. It's literally like a black box. We don't really know exactly how it does it; we just know that if you train it on enough data, it'll learn the mapping from input to output.

AlphaGo had access to two deep networks: the policy network and the value network. The policy network suggested the most promising move. It would take a look at a current board position and say, based on the current position, this is the list of moves I would recommend you consider playing. It also had access to the value network, which would look at a board position and give you a winning probability: what are your chances of winning the game starting from this position? This is exactly the gut feeling; it had its own gut feeling on whether the position is good or bad.

Once you have access to these two networks, you can play in your imagination a number of games. You can consider the most promising moves, then your opponent's most promising moves, and evaluate each move with the value network. You can use a method called minimax: I want to win the game, but I know my opponent wants to win the game, so I want to pick a move that will maximize my chances of winning, knowing that my opponent will try to maximize their chance of winning. If you simulate a bunch of moves, you can get the optimal action. The way to do this imagination, planning, this search in the most efficient way is by using a tree search method called Monte Carlo Tree Search, or MCTS. Whenever people talk about MCTS, they mean this heuristic of how do I choose which futures to consider so I can make informed decisions?

items.question: Why do you see building AlphaGo as mostly an engineering marvel?
items.object: The engineering challenge of building AlphaGo
items.answer: AlphaGo was not just a research challenge, but mostly an engineering marvel. The early versions ran on 1,000 CPUs and 176 GPUs, and the version that played against Lee Sedol used 48 TPUs. These were the first custom accelerators, and they were really primitive back then because it was the first version. The later accelerators are much better and more stable. The system had to be highly optimized to minimize latency and maximize throughput. We had to build large-scale infrastructure for training these networks, and it was a massive endeavor that required a lot of coordinated effort from many talented individuals working on different aspects of the project. I just walked you through a number of steps to obtain the policy network and the value network, and each of these steps had to be implemented at the limits of what was available and possible back then in terms of scale, and in a way where people could think of ideas, try the best ideas fast, and get results fast.

items.question: What did AlphaGo’s Move 37 against Lee Sedol reveal to you about its understanding of Go and its creativity?
items.object: AlphaGo’s Move 37 in game two against Lee Sedol
items.answer: Move 37 in game two against Lee was literally a spectacular moment, in the sense that it showcased to the world that AlphaGo has creativity and demonstrated that AI could come up with strategy that even top human players hadn't considered. At first, I still remember that we thought AlphaGo made an error, that it had hallucinated and done something it didn't mean to do. But then it turned out to be a brilliant, unconventional move that underscored that the system had a deep understanding of the game and creativity. It could think of things that people hadn't thought of before.

items.question: How do you interpret Lee Sedol’s move 78 in game four against AlphaGo?
items.object: Lee Sedol’s move 78 against AlphaGo in game four
items.answer: I think Lee Sedol's move in game four was literally a testament to human ingenuity. Move 78 was unexpected and caught AlphaGo off guard. Initially, AlphaGo misinterpreted it as a mistake and thought it was actually winning, so that's why it didn't respond appropriately. This highlighted a blind spot in the system. The game showed that while systems like AlphaGo are extremely powerful, they still have vulnerabilities and areas where you could further improve them.

items.question: How did you approach fixing the blind spots AlphaGo showed in its games against Lee Sedol?
items.object: Improving AlphaGo’s blind spots after its games against Lee Sedol
items.answer: By the end of the games with Lee Sedol, we put together a benchmark where you're trying to quantify and measure the mistakes that AlphaGo makes and these blind spots, and then we tried a number of approaches to improve the algorithm. The most effective way of getting rid of them was to do what we were doing, just at a higher scale and better. We changed the architecture of the model, switched to a deep residual net with two output heads, and had a bigger network trained on more data. Then we moved to AlphaZero and better algorithms, which made it so that we didn't have hallucinations anymore. In a way, scale and data, the well-known recipe in AI, solved it.

items.question: Why do you see self-play as sufficient to provide the high-quality training data needed to improve AlphaGo?
items.object: Self-play as a source of high-quality Go training data
items.answer: What mattered was that we solved it using self-play. We had access to the most competent Go player in the world and used it to generate the best quality games, then trained on these games. We didn't need human experts because we had an expert in house.

items.question: Why do you consider AlphaZero a game changer compared with AlphaGo?
items.object: AlphaZero's advance over AlphaGo
items.answer: AlphaZero was a game changer because it learned entirely from scratch through self-play without any human data. This was a major leap from AlphaGo, because AlphaGo relied heavily on human expert games. Two things happened. First, AlphaZero managed to simplify the training process and showed that AI can get from zero to superhuman performance purely by playing against itself. That allowed it to be applicable to a whole range of new domains that were out of reach because there wasn't enough human data. I think the more important thing is that we saw AlphaZero also solved all the issues that AlphaGo had in terms of hallucinations, blind spots, and robustness. AlphaZero was a better method, just from the start.

items.question: How do you see AlphaZero’s training process as a model for today’s work on test-time compute and synthetic data?
items.object: AlphaZero’s training process and its connection to test-time compute and synthetic data
items.answer:
AlphaZero, like AlphaGo, uses a policy network and value network along with Monte Carlo Tree Search, so in that respect it's exactly the same. The key difference is in training: AlphaZero starts with random weights and learns by playing games against itself. The main idea behind AlphaZero is that whenever you take a set of weights, a set of policy and value nets, and combine them with search, you end up with a better player. You increase your performance and become a stronger player. That meant we could use this mechanism to improve the model policy. In reinforcement learning, we call it a policy improvement operator: you take an existing policy, do some magic, and come up with a better policy. Then you can distill it back to the initial policy and repeat this process; then you have a reinforcement learning algorithm.

I think this is exactly what people are trying to do today with test-time compute or synthetic data: how can I take a policy, do something with it, planning, search, compute, whatever it is, and derive a better policy which I can then imitate and distill back to the original policy? This is exactly what AlphaZero is doing. It uses MCTS search to produce a better policy, then takes its trajectories, trains this policy and value network on the new, better trajectories, and repeats this process until it converges to an expert level Go player.

items.question: Why do you see MuZero’s approach to learning a world model as a meaningful advance over AlphaZero?
items.object: MuZero’s approach to learning a world model
items.answer:
With AlphaZero, we had a massive success in games like chess, Go, and shogi, where we had access to the game rules, a perfect simulator of the world. But these two assumptions about the perfect simulator made it challenging to apply to real world problems. Real world problems are often messy, lack clear rules, and it's really hard to write a perfect simulator of them. That's exactly what MuZero tried to solve. MuZero mastered games like Go, chess, and shogi, but also mastered more visually challenging games, games like Atari, without having access to the simulator. It learns how to build an internal simulator of the world and then uses this internal simulator in a way similar to what AlphaZero was doing.

It does that by using model-based reinforcement learning. You can take trajectories generated by an agent and try to learn a prediction model of how the world works. This is quite similar to what methods like Sora are trying to do now, where they take YouTube videos and try to learn a world model by predicting, starting from one frame, what's going to happen in future frames. MuZero tries to do exactly that, but differently from generative models: it tries to only model things that matter for solving the reinforcement learning problem. It tries to predict what the reward is going to be in the future, the value of future states, and the policy for future states, only things you need within your MCTS. The fundamentals remain the same: learn a model based on trajectories, and then once you have this model, combine it with search and get superhuman performance.

Of course, you can decouple the two problems and have the model trained separately from data out in the wild, then combine that with MuZero. We found that back then, given the limitations of our models and smaller sizes, it made more sense to keep those two together and only have the model predict things that matter for planning instead of trying to model everything, because you were hitting the limits of what the model capacity could take.

items.object: MuZero-like methods for world modeling and planning
items.answer: I think anything that tries to build a model of how the world works and then use that for planning is within MuZero-like methods. You can train it on YouTube videos, inputs coming from robots, or any environment. You can even think of language models as a form of model of text. They model text, but the thing about text is that the model is a bit trivial; there aren't many artifacts happening when you're trying to predict what the next word is going to be.

items.question: How do you see the adoption of AlphaZero and MuZero beyond games?
items.object: Adoption of AlphaZero and MuZero beyond games
items.answer: I think AlphaZero are quite general methods. There are a number of scientific communities: in chemistry, there's AlphaChem; in quantum computing, some people tried to use AlphaZero in optimization, where they adopted AlphaZero because it was really powerful in planning and solving optimization problems. At the same time, MuZero was incorporated in a version of Tesla's self-driving system. It was reported at their AI Day, and I think it's currently being used within YouTube as a recommendation algorithm. I think it's early days, and it takes time for these new technologies to be fully adopted by industry.

items.question: Why do you see reinforcement learning as essential to continued AI progress once high-quality human training data runs out?
items.object: Reinforcement learning as a way to sustain AI progress beyond human training data
items.answer:
First of all, I think LLMs and multimodal models have brought incredible progress to AI. These models are exceptionally powerful and can perform some truly impressive tasks, but they have some fundamental limitations. One of them is the availability of human data. People keep talking about the data wall and what happens once you run out of high quality data. This is exactly where reinforcement learning shines. Reinforcement learning excels because it doesn't rely solely on pre-existing human data. Instead, it uses experience generated by the agent itself to improve its performance. This self-generated experience allows reinforcement learning to learn and adapt, even to scenarios where human data is scarce or nonexistent.

If you define the reward, the reinforcement learning problem, in the right setting and in the right way, you can effectively exchange compute for intelligence. items.question: How do you think about adapting reinforcement learning methods to large language models?
items.object: Adapting reinforcement learning to large language models
items.answer: We used to say in DeepMind that you have the problem and you have the solution. The problem setting of reinforcement learning is: how do I take a model, a policy, and generate synthetic data? How do I find a way to improve this policy by interacting with the environment through trial and error? That's the reinforcement learning problem setting. Then there's the solution space, where you have value functions and reinforcement learning methods. There's a lot of inspiration to draw from classical reinforcement learning methods developed in the past decade, but you have to adapt them to the new world of LLMs. Methods like Q* try to do that by taking the idea that if I have a policy and do planning, consider possible future scenarios, and have a way to evaluate which one is better, then I can take the best ones and ask the model to imitate them. This is a way of improving the policy. In the classic RL framework, you do that using a policy and a value network. In the new world, you do it by having a reward model or asking your LLM to give you feedback on an output it gave you.

items.question: How do you think about the prospects for using synthetic data to improve AI models?
items.object: Synthetic data for improving AI models
items.answer:
Synthetic data is something we have to solve one way or another. It's not about whether you're bullish or not; it's an obstacle, but we have to find a way around it. We'll run out of data. There's so much data humans can produce, and it's important that these systems start taking actions and learning from their own mistakes. We need to find a way to make synthetic data work.

What people have done is tried the most naive approach, where you take the models, they produce something, and you train on that. Of course, they've seen mode collapse, and this doesn't work out of the box. But new methods never work out of the box; you need to invest in it, take your time, and think of the best way of doing it. I'm really optimistic that we'll find ways to improve these models. There are a number of methods out there, like Q* and the equivalents.

items.question: Why do you think reinforcement learning is necessary to improve language models’ reasoning?
items.object: Reinforcement learning for improving language models’ reasoning
items.answer: I think you need reinforcement learning to get better reasoning, because the distribution of data matters. You have a lot of data out in the wild on the internet, but at the same time you don't always have the right type of data. You don't have data where someone reasons and explains the reasoning in detail. You have some of it, and it's incredible that the models have managed to pick it up and imitate it. But if you want to improve on that capability, you need to do that through reinforcement learning. You need to show the model how this emerging capability can further be improved by having it generate data, interact with the environment, and tell it when it's doing something right and when it's not doing something right.

items.question: How do you understand the legacy of AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and MuZero for building AI agents today?
items.object: The legacy of AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and MuZero for AI agents
items.answer:
I think AlphaGo and MuZero have fundamentally transformed our approach to AI agents because they highlight the importance of planning and scale. If you look at the charts of different models and how they scale, AlphaGo and AlphaZero were really ahead of their time. They were outliers: you had the scaling of compute and then AlphaZero standing on its own. It showed that if you can scale and really push on that, you can get incredible results.
At the same time, it showed that you don't have to only train; you can also have better performance during inference, during test, during evaluation, by using planning. I think this is something we'll start seeing more and more in the near future: methods will start thinking, planning more before making decisions. This is more of the heritage of AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and MuZero. The basic principles are that scale matters, planning matters, and these methods can solve problems we thought were insanely complex or beyond what we can solve on our own. Similar problems with large language models are things we saw back in 2016: these models can hallucinate, but they're also creative and come up with solutions we hadn't thought of. They can also have blind spots, hallucinate, or be susceptible to adversarial attacks, which everyone now knows these neural networks suffer from.

items.question: What do you see as the biggest open question for LLM-based agents in light of AlphaGo's reliability?
items.object: Robustness and reliability of LLM-based agents
items.answer: With AlphaGo, we managed to have insanely robust and reliable systems that would always play Go at the highest possible level and consistently achieve it. AlphaGo Master played against 60 people in online matches and literally won every single one of them. There were these patterns: it was consistent, robust, reliable. I think this is exactly what we're missing now with these LLM based agents. Sometimes they get it, sometimes they don't. You cannot trust them. You have some amazing demos, but they happen once every two times, or once every ten times; the remaining nine, they lost their way and didn't do anything. What we need to do is find a way to make these LLM based agents equally robust to the ones we had with AlphaGo, MuZero, and AlphaZero. This is the new open question.

items.question: How do you understand the promise of in-context learning for AI systems?
items.object: In-context learning
items.answer: I'm excited about in-context learning. It's the idea that a system can learn how to do a new task with few-shot prompting. It sees a few examples and on the fly learns how to adapt to a new environment. It learns how to use the new tools that were provided to it. It's not just all the knowledge stored in systems, but it can also acquire new knowledge by interacting with the real world, interacting with the environment. This is another place where there's a lot of work happening at the moment, and there's going to be amazing progress in the next couple of years.

items.question: What do you see as the best way to make AI models reliable?
items.object: Reliability through recovery from mistakes
items.answer: The best way to achieve reliability is to ensure that these models somehow know how to recover from their mistakes. Along with planning and in-context learning, this is one of the three areas I'm really excited to see progress on.

items.question: What do you see as startups’ advantages when competing with established AI research labs?
items.object: Startups’ advantages over established AI research labs
items.answer: It's a new world for me, but at the same time it's not that new because when I joined DeepMind, it was literally a startup, and I was in the first 10 employees. I saw that firsthand. One of the benefits of working for a startup is the agility and the focus. Everyone really cares, everyone moves really fast, and there's a clear focus on what we want to build. Building is the most important motivation for people. This is one of the big advantages startups have over more established businesses. It's easier to adapt to new findings and technologies. You're not tied to preexisting solutions or products that you don't want to deprecate because they bring a lot of revenue. As a startup you have no such chains; you can move fast, be innovative, break conventions, and leverage open source resources, things that are out of touch for the big labs. You don't have the red tape that big places tend to have.

items.question: Which AI research milestones do you see as most defining over the past twelve years?
items.object: Major AI research milestones: AlexNet, DQN, AlphaGo, AlphaFold, and GPT-4
items.answer:
I'll give a list of what I think are the main milestones in AI in the past 12 years I've been around. The first one is AlexNet, the first paper that showed deep learning is the answer. Back then it didn't feel like it; it felt like a curiosity. Now I think most people are convinced deep learning is part of the answer.
Then it was DQN. I had the pleasure to work on DQN and see firsthand how it started. It was developed by a friend of mine, Vlad Mnih, and it was the first system that showed you can combine deep learning with reinforcement learning to achieve human or superhuman performance in really complex environments.
Then AlphaGo. I was really lucky to work on that, and it showed that scale and planning are important ingredients. If you do that right, you get huge success in an incredibly complex environment. AlphaFold is another one, again by DeepMind. It showed that these methods aren't just things you can use to solve games, but that they'll make the world a better place. They'll ensure healthcare is improved and scientific discoveries are realized.
Finally, GPT-4. I think GPT-4 is the latest big advancement in AI because it showed that artificial general intelligence is a matter of years; it's within reach. We are getting there. I think most people now believe we're a few years away from AI.
